tip: 'Liten' is irregular: it becomes 'litet' with an ett-word and 'små' in the plural. 'Barnet är litet' uses the ett-form.
Swedish has no separate continuous tense. 'Skiner' covers both 'shines' and 'is shining', so 'solen skiner' means the sun is shining now.
To say where you are from, use 'komma från': 'vi kommer från Göteborg' literally says 'we come from', but it means we are from.
The filler subject stays 'det är' no matter what follows: 'det är varmt'. Learners wrongly reach for 'den är' with en-words.
Many ett-words ending in a consonant look the same in the plural: 'ett ägg', 'tolv ägg'. No ending is added.
For 'ta', the command form is 'ta', the same as the infinitive, so an order is 'ta buss nummer sju'. The present 'tar' is not used to give an order.
When a sentence starts with something other than the subject, the verb still comes second: 'idag äter vi', never 'idag vi äter'.
'Barn' is the same in singular and plural; the definite plural just adds '-en', so 'barnen' means the children.
Weather statements need a filler subject 'det': 'nu börjar det regna'. Here 'det' carries no real meaning of its own.
Adding '-s' to the verb makes it passive: 'väcker' (wakes) becomes 'väcks' (is woken). 'Barnen väcks' means the children get woken.
'Gott om' is a fixed phrase meaning plenty of: 'har gott om tid' means has plenty of time.
After an adjective like 'redo', link the following verb with 'att' plus the infinitive: 'redo att gå' (ready to go).
'Nyligen' means recently. It goes between 'har' and the verb: 'har nyligen kommit' (has recently come).
To prefer one thing to another, use 'föredra X framför Y'. Here 'framför' means 'over, rather than', not physically in front of.
When 'igår' comes first, the verb must come second: 'igår regnade det', never 'igår det regnade'.
'Man' is the generic 'you, one' for what people in general do: 'här kan man köpa biljetter' means here one can buy tickets.
Seasons normally take 'på' plus the definite form: 'på hösten' (in autumn), 'på våren' (in spring).
Use 'mycket' with uncountable nouns like 'skog': 'mycket skog'. For countable things you would switch to 'många' instead.
'Ingå i' means to be included in: 'frukosten ingår i priset' says breakfast is part of the price.
'Det finns' means 'there is' for existence: 'det finns bröd på hyllan'. 'Det är' means 'it is', like 'det är bröd'.
For how long something lasts, use 'i' plus the time span: 'varar i en timme' means lasts for an hour.
To say something has happened, use 'har' plus a special verb form: 'har allt gått bra'. 'Gått' differs from the plain past 'gick'.
'Bör' means ought to or should, a slightly formal recommendation: 'vi bör agera' means we should act.
In passive phrases, 'av' marks who does it, like English 'by': 'omtyckt av alla' means liked by everyone.
'Sin' points back to the subject of the sentence: 'sin favoritstol' means the cat's own chair, not someone else's.
'Bra' never changes form to agree: 'en bra dag', and it stays 'bra' everywhere, unlike 'stor' which becomes 'stort'.
'Dit' means 'to where' and marks movement toward a place; 'där' is for a fixed location. 'Åka' takes 'dit'.
'Hos' means 'at the place of' a person: 'hos vår tandläkare' means at our dentist's.
No word for 'of' sits between a measure and its contents: 'en kopp kaffe' means a cup of coffee, just placed side by side.
When 'känna' means to feel, it needs an extra word for the self: 'du känner dig' means you feel. The 'dig' is required, not optional.
